title: Practice Exam 1 — Mapping, Biomes and Connections
description: Balanced revision paper with topographic mapping, climate, food access, urbanisation and migration stimuli.

topo.title: Stimulus A — Schematic topographic map
topo.text: Use the grid, contour heights, point labels and scale note to answer the questions. Each grid square represents 1 km by 1 km. The map is a purpose-made practice diagram, not a real location.

image.alt: Schematic topographic contour map with eastings 32 to 36 and northings 48 to 52. Point A is at easting 33.2, northing 49.3 and 250 metres. Point B is at easting 34.4, northing 49.9 and 400 metres. Contours are labelled at 50 metre intervals. A north arrow is shown.
image.caption: Contour interval: 50 m. Grid squares: 1 km × 1 km. Scale note: 1:25,000.

climate.title: Stimulus B — Climate graph
climate.text: The graph shows monthly rainfall and mean temperature for an illustrative tropical savanna-style climate. Use the axes and units; bars show rainfall and the line shows temperature.

image.alt: Climate graph with monthly rainfall bars and temperature line. Rainfall is highest early in the year and lowest around July. Temperatures remain warm throughout the year.
image.caption: Illustrative practice dataset; not a measured weather-station record.

food.title: Stimulus D — Food access index
food.text: The chart uses an invented classroom dataset to practise describing global patterns. A higher score means more reliable access to adequate food. Regions are anonymised and are not real country scores.

image.alt: Bar chart of food access scores: Region A 38, Region B 49, Region C 63, Region D 78 and Region E 86. Higher scores represent more reliable food access.
image.caption: Synthetic practice data only; not actual national or regional statistics.

urban.title: Stimulus E — City Z urbanisation trend
urban.text: City Z is fictional. The data have been constructed for exam practice. The urban share is the percentage of the population living in urban areas.

image.alt: Line graph showing City Z urban share rising from 42 percent in 2000 to 70 percent in 2030, while total population rises from 3.2 to 6.8 million.
image.caption: Synthetic practice dataset; City Z is not a real city.

pyramids.title: Stimulus F — Two population pyramids
pyramids.text: The pyramids use invented age-structure data. Compare the width of the base, working-age bands and older age groups.

image.alt: Two population pyramids with age groups from 0–14 to 75+. Population A has a wider base and narrows sharply with age. Population B has a narrower base and proportionally larger middle and older groups.
image.caption: Synthetic data; not actual country population pyramids.

migration.title: Stimulus G — International migration pathways
migration.text: This is a schematic diagram of push and pull factors and two broad forms of movement. It is not a map of a specific route or country.

image.alt: Schematic showing an origin country and a destination country connected by arrows labelled voluntary movement and forced displacement. Push factors include limited jobs, conflict and insecurity; pull factors include employment, safety and services.
image.caption: Conceptual diagram for practice; not a mapped migration route.

questions.stem: Using Stimulus A, what is the four-figure grid reference of point A?
Using Stimulus A, what is the approximate bearing from A to B?
questions.explanation: The change is about 1.285 km east and 0.601 km north, giving a bearing of approximately 065° clockwise from north.

questions.stem: Using Stimulus A, what is the contour interval?
questions.explanation: Adjacent labelled contours increase by 50 m.

questions.stem: Using Stimulus A, what is the aspect of the slope at point A?
questions.explanation: Aspect is the direction a slope faces. Point A is on the south-western side of the hill, so the slope faces south-west.

questions.stem: According to Stimulus B, which month has the lowest rainfall?
questions.explanation: The shortest rainfall bar is in July.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the temperature pattern in Stimulus B?
options: Temperatures remain warm throughout the year
Temperatures remain below 5°C throughout the year
The coldest months receive the most rainfall
questions.explanation: The temperature line stays in a relatively warm range across the year.

questions.stem: Which anonymised region has the highest food access score in Stimulus D?
questions.explanation: Region E has the highest bar and a score of 86.

questions.stem: In Stimulus E, what is City Z’s urban population share in 2030?
questions.explanation: The graph shows an urban share of 70% in 2030.

questions.stem: Which movement in Stimulus G most clearly represents forced displacement?
options: A person moving for a preferred university course
A person leaving because of a serious threat to safety
A person moving for a planned holiday
A person relocating for a promotion by choice
questions.explanation: Forced displacement occurs when people have to leave because of serious threats or circumstances.

questions.stem: Which population structure is suggested by the broad base of Population A in Stimulus F?
options: A relatively high proportion of children
A population made up only of older people
An equal proportion in every age group
questions.explanation: A broad base represents a comparatively large younger age group.

questions.stem: Using Stimulus B, describe the seasonal pattern of rainfall and temperature. Explain how this pattern is consistent with a tropical savanna-style climate. (5 marks)
criteria: Identifies a clear wet-season pattern using one or more early-year months.
Identifies the drier middle-year period, including July as the lowest-rainfall month.
Uses at least two accurate rainfall values or comparisons with units/months.
Describes the relatively warm temperature pattern using the line.
Links distinct wet and dry seasons and warm temperatures to a savanna-style climate.
questions.model: Rainfall is much higher at the start and end of the year, with January receiving about 220 mm, while July is the driest month at about 28 mm. Temperatures remain warm, falling from about 27°C early in the year to about 21°C in July before rising again. A distinct wet and dry season with warm conditions is consistent with a tropical savanna-style climate.

questions.stem: Use Stimulus D to describe one pattern in food access and explain two factors that can contribute to food insecurity. (5 marks)
criteria: Describes the broad difference between lower-scoring and higher-scoring regions.
Uses at least two accurate scores or comparisons from the graph.
Explains one relevant cause such as poverty, conflict, climate hazards or unequal access.
Explains a second relevant cause or challenge such as transport, water scarcity or land degradation.
Links the causes to people’s physical or economic access to sufficient safe and nutritious food.
questions.model: The practice data show lower food access in Regions A and B (38 and 49) than in Regions D and E (78 and 86). Food insecurity can be caused by poverty, because people may not be able to afford adequate food, and by conflict or climate hazards, which can disrupt farming, transport and markets. Water scarcity and land degradation can also reduce food production. Food security depends on access as well as the amount of food produced.

questions.stem: Using Stimulus E, describe the trend in City Z’s urbanisation and explain one possible benefit and one challenge of this growth. (5 marks)
criteria: Describes the increase in urban population share from 2000 to 2030.
Uses at least two accurate values from the graph.
Explains a possible benefit such as access to jobs, education, services or transport.
Explains a possible challenge such as pressure on housing, infrastructure, water or waste services.
Links planning or service provision to how effectively the city manages growth.
questions.model: City Z’s urban share rises from 42% in 2000 to 70% in 2030, while its total population also increases. Urban growth can improve access to employment, education and health services because these are concentrated in cities. However, rapid growth can place pressure on affordable housing, transport, water and sanitation. Planning and investment help determine whether services keep pace with population growth.

questions.stem: Using Stimulus G, explain one push factor and one pull factor for international migration. Then explain one possible impact on an origin country and one on a host country. (5 marks)
criteria: Explains a push factor that encourages departure from an origin country.
Explains a pull factor that attracts people to a destination country.
Explains one possible impact on an origin country.
Explains one possible impact on a host country.
Uses the terms origin and host/destination accurately and links each impact to migration.
questions.model: A lack of employment or insecurity can push people to leave an origin country, while job opportunities or safety can pull them towards a destination. The origin country may receive remittances but could lose some skilled workers. The host country may gain workers and skills, while needing to plan for extra demand for housing and services.

questions.stem: Assess the positive and negative impacts of international migration on both host and origin countries. In your response, refer to migration to Australia, skilled migration and the points-based approach, refugees and asylum seekers, and at least one other international example. (15 marks)
criteria: Introduces a clear judgement about whether international migration is more beneficial, challenging or mixed overall.
Defines international migration accurately as movement across an international border.
Distinguishes voluntary migration from forced migration.
Explains at least one push factor that can encourage people to leave an origin country.
Explains at least one pull factor that can attract people to a destination country.
Explains a positive impact on a host country, such as filling skill shortages or supporting economic activity.
Explains a possible challenge for a host country, such as pressure on housing or services if planning is inadequate.
Explains a positive impact on an origin country, such as remittances or diaspora links.
Explains a possible negative impact on an origin country, such as loss of skilled workers or family separation.
Explains the broad purpose of skilled migration selection in Australia.
Refers to Australia’s points-based approach without inventing a points threshold or guaranteed visa outcome.
Distinguishes a refugee from an asylum seeker accurately.
Uses Australia and at least one other international migration example relevantly.
Uses evidence or stimulus information to support the discussion rather than listing impacts only.
Finishes with a reasoned conclusion that weighs impacts on both origin and host countries.
questions.model:
International migration is the movement of people across an international border to live in another country. Its effects are mixed because it can create opportunities for migrants and destination countries, while also producing challenges for origin countries and communities. Voluntary migrants may move for employment, education or family reasons, whereas forced migrants leave because of serious threats such as conflict or persecution. A refugee is outside their country and meets the relevant protection definition; an asylum seeker has requested protection and is waiting for a decision.

In a host country such as Australia, skilled migration can help address labour shortages, contribute to economic activity and add skills and cultural knowledge. Australia's skilled migration settings include a points-based pathway, which is designed to select applicants against relevant criteria; meeting a points threshold alone should not be described as a guaranteed visa. Migration can also increase demand for housing, schools, health care and transport when population growth is not matched by planning and investment.

Origin countries may benefit when migrants send remittances to relatives, maintain business links or return with new skills. However, the departure of trained workers can contribute to a loss of skills, and migration can separate families. The Mexico–USA corridor is an international example in which employment, family links, border rules and the risks of irregular movement can all shape migration decisions. Humanitarian migration provides a different example because safety and protection, rather than simply seeking better employment, are central. Overall, migration is not automatically positive or negative: its effects depend on who moves, why they move, the rights and conditions they experience, and how well origin and host countries plan for change.
